title: How One Ohio Town Became the Center of the Data Center Debate
summary:
In the small Ohio village of Mt. Orab, farmland next to family homes has become the center of a statewide debate. Property records show that about 1,000 acres of farmland and trees there were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025. Construction has not begun yet, and it is not clear when it will start.

Leading the local pushback is Nick Owens, a lifelong Republican and small-town attorney from nearby Brown County. He says nondisclosure agreements have made it hard for residents to learn details about the project. He teamed up with another local attorney and a real estate agent who shared his worries, and together they helped build Conserve Ohio, a volunteer network reaching nearly all of Ohio's 88 counties, with Democrats, Republicans, and independents.

This fall, the group is backing ballot measures in 10 communities that would change local charters to block large-scale data centers, the huge computing sites used to power artificial intelligence. It is also collecting signatures for a proposed amendment to the state constitution that would ban such centers across Ohio, aiming to put it before voters in 2027.

Supporters point to benefits such as tax revenue, money for schools, and construction jobs, though the number of permanent jobs is smaller. Critics, including Owens, worry about secrecy, constant noise, pollution, and new power plants the sites may require. Owens says he would consider placing data centers on old industrial sites, away from homes, instead of on farmland.

The issue has also entered Ohio's race for the U.S. Senate, where former Senator Sherrod Brown and incumbent Senator Jon Husted have traded criticism over past support for data centers. Meanwhile, volunteers like Linda Moodie, an independent, are collecting signatures at community events, including a Halloween celebration in Fairfield on October 22.
why_it_matters: Where large computing sites are built affects nearby homes, farmland, and electricity use, so local votes and state rules can shape whole communities.

background_read: Data centers are large sites filled with computers that store information and run online services, including tools that use artificial intelligence.
Because they need a lot of space and electricity, building one near homes can raise questions about noise, pollution, and new power plants.
A local charter sets the basic rules for a community, and voters can sometimes change those rules through ballot measures.
A state constitution sets the basic rules for a whole state, and changing it usually starts with collecting signatures and putting the question to voters.
